claims.claim: A naive observer is more interesting because he gives only what he has seen, whereas adult witnesses cannot separate what they saw from what it means.
claims.quote: he's just giving you what he has seen

claims.feature: perfect memory and daily amnesia as inverse designs
claims.claim: Having built Severian to forget nothing, Wolfe built Latro from a real brain injury to forget everything.
claims.quote: let's do one of these guys who forgets everything

claims.claim: Every narrator is unreliable because each sees from his own standpoint and not another's.
claims.quote: They're all unreliable. Well, we all are, aren't we?

claims.feature: epistolary entry with per-writer style shifts
claims.claim: He recommends The Sorcerer's House as an entry point because the epistolary form helps readers, provided they accept the style changing with each letter writer.
claims.quote: the style changes from one letter writer to another

claims.claim: Military service teaches you to look at scenery as defensive positions, the perception behind Severian's line that war is a new geography.
claims.quote: look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions

claims.claim: Wolfe learned prose from a college editor who blue-pencilled every word a sentence did not require, and he wrote the next story so it could not be cut.
claims.quote: taking out every word the sentence

claims.claim: His definition of good literature is what an educated reader can read and reread with increased pleasure, and he refuses to write fiction that gives everything up on first reading.
He will not adjudicate readers' theories about the text because he argues from presumed expertise on an unlevel field, and there is no sacredness to the text.
Wolfe says readers will see things in the books he does not see consciously, and that he likes those things.

claims.feature: Peace built on lies (Gaiman) vs. 'I never lie'
claims.claim: Gaiman calls Wolfe the master of lying in fiction and says Peace is built on lies decipherable after three or four readings; Wolfe replies that he never lies.

claims.feature: fiction as assurance that things need not be as they are
claims.claim: The most important thing fiction does is assure the reader that things need not be as they are now, which Wolfe names hope.
claims.quote: the most important thing is hope

claims.claim: Anything in a book must do several things at once (tone, plot, character); a 'pass the salt' line is waste unless said in a particular way or for a purpose.
claims.quote: you really have to be doing several things at once

claims.claim: Wolfe denies his style has changed at all: he writes in a voice appropriate to the story he has to tell.
claims.quote: I write in a voice appropriate to the story

claims.claim: A style becomes difficult only when it is not suited to what is being said; if it is the right style he likes it, if not he changes it.
claims.quote: A style becomes difficult when it is not suited

claims.claim: Character speech comes from listening to what people actually say as well as what they mean; Remora and Incus are slight exaggerations of real people, and Oreb manages only two syllables.
claims.quote: what they actually say as well as what they mean

verdicts.trueWording: "he's just giving you what he has seen"
verdicts.note: Raw MIT Tech Review page fetched with a browser UA (200, 468KB). Wolfe: "I think a naive observer is more interesting to read because he's just giving you what he has seen. If you've ever listened to people giving testimony at a trial, they are almost incapable of distinguishing between what they have actually seen or heard and their opinions of what it means." Quote verbatim. Wording note: the page says "people giving testimony at a trial", not literally "adult witnesses" — the child/adult contrast is the question's frame (young narrators, "what Maisie knew"); substance of the limb is fully supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "In Severian, I had created a character who forgot nothing"
verdicts.note: Same page. Wolfe: "I came across an article about a brain injury that is perfectly real [anterograde amnesia]... In Severian, I had created a character who forgot nothing. And I thought: let's do one of these guys who forgets everything." The interviewer frames it as "In the Soldier series you created a narrator who forgets everything at the end of every day"; the same page names Latro as the Soldier series narrator, so the Latro identification is page-supported. Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "You see things from your standpoint and not from... someone else"
verdicts.note: Same page. Q: "A persistent theme of your writing is the unreliability of narrators." Wolfe: "They're all unreliable. Well, we all are, aren't we?" Then, to "Everyone's story is necessarily subjective": "You see things from your standpoint and not from the standpoint of someone else." Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "It's an epistolary novel, and that seems to help people along"
verdicts.note: Same page, EDITING AND WRITING section, answering how a Niven/Card/Brin reader should start Wolfe: "I think it's probably The Sorcerer's House. It's an epistolary novel, and that seems to help people along. So long as they don't get bothered by the fact that the style changes from one letter writer to another." Every limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "You learn to look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions"
verdicts.note: Same page, WAR AND RELIGION section. The interviewer quotes Severian's passage ("War is not a new experience; it is a new world ... Even its geography is new, because it is a geography in which insignificant hills and hollows are lifted to the importance of cities") and Wolfe's whole reply is the quoted line. The claim's link between the Severian passage and the perception is by direct adjacency (reply to that quoted passage), not an explicit statement; the military framing is the section's own ("What military service does is rub off a lot of the pretense and self-deception").

verdicts.trueWording: "He's taking out every word the sentence doesn't require"
verdicts.note: locusmag.com/2002/Issue09/GaimanWolfe.html fetched raw (200, 17KB; page uses a legacy charset so curly apostrophes render as replacement chars — normalized before matching). Wolfe on the student editor of The Commentator at Texas A&M: "he got a blue pencil, and he edited it there in front of me... 'I see what he's doing. He's taking out every word the sentence doesn't require. I'm going to write the next story so he can't do that.'" Also "I learned more from the student editor of The Commentator than I have ever learned from any other editor." All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "read by an educated reader, and reread with increased pleasure"
verdicts.note: Same Locus page. Gaiman quotes Wolfe's own letter definition: "My definition of good literature is that which can be read by an educated reader, and reread with increased pleasure." On fiction that gives everything up first time, Wolfe: "Phooey! I don't want to write that kind of thing. Rats! I don't like it and it would bore me to write it and I'm not gonna write it." Both limbs supported; the definition is Wolfe's, quoted back to him by Gaiman.

verdicts.trueWording: "I am dealing from this position of presumed expertise"
verdicts.note: Same Locus page: "too often people want me to go in and settle their argument. That's exactly what I should not do. I am dealing from this position of presumed expertise. We don't have a level playing field... There's no sacredness to the text." Every limb verbatim, including the Baker Street Irregulars analogy that carries it.

verdicts.trueWording: "You're going to see things in there that I don't see consciously"
verdicts.note: Same Locus page: "And besides, I don't know everything to give it up. You're going to see things in there that I don't see consciously. I like those things." Quote and both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "Peace is built on lies" / "I never lie."
verdicts.note: Same Locus page. Gaiman: "I think Gene is the master of lying in fiction, both directly and indirectly. Peace is built on lies... After three or four times through that text, you begin to be able to say, 'I think he's lying about this or that.'" Wolfe's entire reply: "I never lie." All three limbs (master of lying, Peace built on lies, three or four readings, the reply) verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "it assures the reader that things need not be as they are now"
verdicts.note: Same Locus page. Q: "What's the most important thing about fiction?" Wolfe: "The most important thing is that it assures the reader that things need not be as they are now. In other words, the most important thing is hope." Every limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "it's a waste unless it's said in some particular way"
verdicts.note: locusmag.com/2011/03/gene-wolfe-engineering-the-future/ fetched raw (200, 163KB); page is the excerpts from the March 2011 Locus interview. Wolfe: "When you do anything in a book, you really have to be doing several things at once. You need to pique the tone of the book; to move the plot forward; to touch on the character of the person. If you've got a dinner scene where somebody says, 'Pass the salt,' it's a waste unless it's said in some particular way, or the character wants the salt for some special purpose." Every limb verbatim, tone/plot/character included.

Wayback capture 20020703232613 of sfsite.com/03b/gw124.htm fetched raw (200, 41KB); header confirms "A Magus Of Many Suns: An Interview With Gene Wolfe / An interview with Nick Gevers / January 2002". Wolfe: "My style hasn't changed at all. I write in a voice appropriate to the story I have to tell, that's all. I may be doing it a bit better now, or a bit worse; but that's always been the idea." Both limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "I use the style suited to the story... If it isn't, I change it"
verdicts.note: Same SF Site capture: "There really aren't any answers. I use the style suited to the story. If it's the right style for the story, I like it. If it isn't, I change it. A style becomes difficult when it is not suited to what is being said." Quote and both limbs verbatim. Wording note: the page says "becomes difficult when it is not suited"; the claim's "only when" is a (fair, context-consistent) tightening, not the page's word.

Same SF Site capture: "I listen to people, what they actually say as well as what they mean, and how they say it. Both Patera Remora and Patera Incus speak as slight exaggerations of people I've met." And: "Oreb [the night chough, a talking bird] talks, but Oreb can manage only two syllables: 'Good bird! Watch out! Bad boy. Iron girl. Good Silk!'" All three limbs verbatim.
